title: Elements and Compounds
seo_title: Grade 8 Science: Elements and Compounds Worksheets (MATATAG)
standard_text: Elements and compounds are pure substances; compounds are formed from elements in fixed ratios and represented by chemical formulas; physical and chemical properties. (summary of the MATATAG Science curriculum, Grade 8, Quarter 2: Science of Materials)
meta_desc: Free Grade 8 Science worksheets (MATATAG, Quarter 2: Science of Materials): pure substances and mixtures, physical and chemical properties, physical and chemical changes, chemical formulas and compounds in everyday products. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: A compound is two or more elements chemically joined in a fixed ratio.
key_sub: The formula tells you which atoms and how many: H₂O has 2 H and 1 O.
body_html:
How to think about it

Matter is either a pure substance (an element or a compound) or a mixture. An element has only one kind of atom; a compound has two or more elements joined in a fixed ratio and can only be separated by a chemical change. Mixtures can be separated by physical means such as filtering or evaporating.

Physical properties (color, density, melting point) can be observed without changing the substance; chemical properties (flammability, reaction with acid) describe how it changes into new substances. Signs of a chemical change include a new color, a gas, a precipitate, light or a temperature change that is hard to reverse.

Example

How many atoms are in one molecule of glucose, C₆H₁₂O₆?

6 + 12 + 6

Answer: 24

Example

Is rusting iron a physical or a chemical change?

A new substance (iron oxide) forms.

Answer: chemical change

Common mistakes

  • Calling melting ice a chemical change.
  • Thinking a mixture of iron and sulfur is the compound iron sulfide.
  • Reading the subscript as applying to the atom before and after it (in CO₂ the 2 is for O only).

faq.q: Why must household cleaners never be mixed?
faq.a: Some mixtures, such as bleach with ammonia or acid, react to give toxic gases.

faq.q: What is the difference between an atom and a molecule?
faq.a: An atom is a single particle of an element; a molecule is two or more atoms joined together.

items.q: Emmanuel writes 3NH<sub>3</sub>. How many hydrogen atoms are there in all?
items.e: The coefficient 3 multiplies everything: 3 × 3 = 9.

items.q: Kristine looks up calcium carbonate (chalk), CaCO<sub>3</sub>. How many atoms are in one molecule?
items.e: 1 calcium + 1 carbon + 3 oxygen = 5 atoms.

items.q: Kyla studies hydrogen burning: 2H2 + O2 → 2H2O. How many oxygen atoms are in the reactants (left side)?
items.e: Multiply each coefficient by the subscript and add. The number is the same on both sides: 2.

items.q: Kristine studies magnesium burning: 2Mg + O2 → 2MgO. How many oxygen atoms are in the reactants (left side)?
items.e: Multiply each coefficient by the subscript and add. The number is the same on both sides: 2.

items.q: Na<sup>+</sup> and P<sup>3−</sup> ions combine. What is the formula of the compound?
items.e: Use the lowest numbers that make the total charge zero: 3 × (+1) + 1 × (−3) = 0.

items.q: Lance looks up ethanol, C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub>O. How many atoms are in one molecule?
items.e: 2 carbon + 6 hydrogen + 1 oxygen = 9 atoms.

items.q: Hazel writes 3H<sub>2</sub>O. How many hydrogen atoms are there in all?
items.e: The coefficient 3 multiplies everything: 3 × 2 = 6.

items.q: Lance studies making salt: 2Na + Cl2 → 2NaCl. How many chlorine atoms are in the products (right side)?
items.e: Multiply each coefficient by the subscript and add. The number is the same on both sides: 2.

items.q: What is the formula of barium fluoride?
items.e: Barium forms Ba<sup>2+</sup> and fluorine forms F<sup>−</sup>; the charges must add to zero.

items.q: Vincent looks up oxygen gas, O<sub>2</sub>. How many atoms are in one molecule?
items.e: 2 oxygen = 2 atoms.

items.q: Carlo writes 2C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>8</sub>. How many carbon atoms are there in all?
items.e: The coefficient 2 multiplies everything: 2 × 3 = 6.

items.q: How many hydrogen atoms are in one molecule of methane, CH<sub>4</sub>?
items.e: The subscript after H is 4.

items.q: Mae writes 2H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>. How many oxygen atoms are there in all?
items.e: The coefficient 2 multiplies everything: 2 × 4 = 8.

items.q: Jose studies photosynthesis: 6CO2 + 6H2O → C6H12O6 + 6O2. How many hydrogen atoms are in the products (right side)?
items.e: Multiply each coefficient by the subscript and add. The number is the same on both sides: 12.

items.q: Kyla studies rusting of iron: 4Fe + 3O2 → 2Fe2O3. How many oxygen atoms are in the reactants (left side)?
items.e: Multiply each coefficient by the subscript and add. The number is the same on both sides: 6.

items.q: Rodel writes 2H<sub>2</sub>O. How many oxygen atoms are there in all?
items.e: The coefficient 2 multiplies everything: 2 × 1 = 2.

items.q: Kenneth looks up ozone, O<sub>3</sub>. How many atoms are in one molecule?

items.q: Renz writes 4H<sub>2</sub>O. How many hydrogen atoms are there in all?
items.e: The coefficient 4 multiplies everything: 4 × 2 = 8.

items.q: What is the formula of potassium phosphide?

items.q: What is the name of AlF<sub>3</sub>?
items.e: Name the metal, then the non-metal with -ide. Ionic names do not use prefixes.

items.q: What kind of bond forms between iodine (I) and chlorine (Cl)?

items.q: What happens when red and blue litmus paper are dipped into an acidic solution?

Blue litmus turns red; red litmus stays red.
